stem: In a plain React 19 client app (no framework), which two make the nearest `<Suspense>` boundary show its fallback while data or code loads? (Choose two.)

options.text: Rendering a `lazy()` component whose code has not finished downloading
options.why: lazy() throws its pending import to the nearest boundary until the module resolves.

options.text: Reading a cached, still-pending promise with `use(promise)` during render
options.why: use() suspends the component until the promise settles, so the boundary shows its fallback.

options.text: Starting a `fetch` inside `useEffect` and storing the result in state
options.why: Effects run after commit, so the component has already rendered; Suspense never learns about that request.

options.text: Calling `setTimeout` in an event handler before updating state
options.why: Timers do not suspend rendering; the state update simply happens later.

options.text: Setting an `isLoading` flag in state and returning `null` while it is true
options.why: Returning null is ordinary rendering. It shows nothing, not the boundary fallback.

explanation: Only Suspense-enabled sources suspend: lazy-loaded components, use() on a promise, and frameworks that integrate with Suspense (such as Next.js or Relay). Data fetched in an effect is invisible to Suspense because the component has already rendered and committed by the time the effect runs.

stem: In React 19 you can write an error boundary as a function component by catching errors with a built-in hook.

options.text: True
options.why: There is still no hook equivalent of getDerivedStateFromError or componentDidCatch.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: error boundaries must be class components. Libraries such as react-error-boundary wrap that class for you.

explanation: An error boundary is a class component that implements static getDerivedStateFromError (to render fallback UI) and/or componentDidCatch (to log). React 19 adds root-level callbacks such as onCaughtError, but there is still no hook for catching render errors in a function component.
reference: react.dev: Catching rendering errors with an error boundary

stem: A page renders `<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}><Chart /></Suspense>`, where `Chart` comes from `lazy(() => import('./Chart'))`. What does the user see the first time this renders, before the chart code has downloaded?

options.text: A blank area, because lazy components render `null` until their code arrives
options.why: lazy components do not render null; they suspend and let the boundary decide what to show.

options.text: The `<Spinner />` fallback, which React swaps for `<Chart />` once the module loads
options.why: The nearest Suspense boundary shows its fallback while the lazy component is suspended.

options.text: An error, because `lazy` needs its own error boundary to work at all
options.why: Error boundaries handle failed imports, but loading itself is handled by Suspense.

options.text: The page freezes until the chunk downloads, because imports block the main thread
options.why: Dynamic import is asynchronous; React keeps the rest of the page interactive.

explanation: A lazy component suspends on first render while its dynamic import is pending. The closest <Suspense> ancestor renders its fallback, and React retries the render once the module promise resolves.

stem: What does the first value returned by `const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()` tell you?

options.text: Whether a transition started by this hook is still in progress
options.why: isPending is true while React works on (or waits for) the transition's updates.

options.text: Whether any component in the app is currently suspended on data
options.why: isPending only tracks transitions started through this hook's startTransition.

options.text: Whether the browser main thread is currently busy running JavaScript
options.why: React does not expose main-thread busyness; isPending is about React updates.

options.text: Whether the last transition failed and should be retried by the caller
options.why: Errors in a transition go to an error boundary; isPending does not report failure.

explanation: useTransition returns isPending and startTransition. Updates inside startTransition are non-blocking; while they are rendering or suspended, isPending is true, so you can show a subtle indicator (such as dimming) while the old UI stays on screen.

stem: Type the name of the React hook that returns a version of a value that may "lag behind" during urgent updates, so expensive or suspending UI can render it in the background: `const deferredQuery = ________(query);`
explanation: useDeferredValue first renders with the old value, then re-renders in the background with the new value. Urgent updates (like typing) stay responsive while the slower part catches up.

stem: Where should `const Settings = lazy(() => import('./Settings'))` be written?

options.text: Inside the component that renders `<Settings />`, so the import only runs when needed
options.why: Calling lazy() during render creates a new component type each time, so React remounts it and loses its state.

options.text: At the top level of a module, outside any component
options.why: Declared once at module level, the lazy component keeps a stable identity across renders.

options.text: Inside a `useEffect`, so the chunk downloads after the first paint
options.why: Effects run after rendering; a lazy component must already exist when React renders it.

options.text: Inside `useMemo` with an empty dependency array, which React requires for lazy()
options.why: useMemo is not required, and React may discard memoized values; module scope is the documented place.

explanation: React compares element types by identity. A lazy() call inside a component returns a new type on every render, which resets the subtree and re-suspends. Declare lazy components once at the top level of a module.

stem: Match each React API with what it is for.

options.text: Show a fallback while part of the tree is waiting for code or data
options.why: Suspense boundary.

options.text: Mark a state update as non-urgent so it can be interrupted
options.why: Transitions.

options.text: Read the value of a promise or context during render
options.why: use().

options.text: Replace a crashed subtree with fallback UI
options.why: Error boundary.

explanation: Suspense handles waiting, transitions handle priority, use() reads promises (and context) in render, and error boundaries handle failures. Together they let React show stable UI while work is pending.

options.text: The boundary catches the error and renders its fallback UI in place of `Save`
options.why: Boundaries only catch errors during rendering, lifecycles and effects of their children, not event handlers.

options.text: The boundary does not catch it; the error is reported and the button stays on screen
options.why: Event handlers run outside rendering, so the error propagates like any other JavaScript error.

options.text: React unmounts the whole root, because uncaught errors always tear down the app
options.why: React unmounts the root only for errors thrown during rendering that no boundary catches.

options.text: React swallows the error silently, because event handler errors are ignored
options.why: The error still surfaces (in the console and window error handlers); React just does not show a boundary fallback.

explanation: Error boundaries catch errors thrown while React renders, in lifecycle methods and in effects of their descendants. An event handler runs later, outside rendering, so use try/catch in the handler (or set an error state) to show error UI.

stem: Which of these errors will an error boundary placed above the component NOT catch? (Choose three.)

options.text: An error thrown inside a `setTimeout` callback scheduled by a child
options.why: Asynchronous callbacks run outside React's render, so no boundary sees them.

options.text: An error thrown inside a child's `onClick` handler
options.why: Event handlers are not part of rendering.

options.text: An error thrown in the error boundary's own `render` method
options.why: A boundary cannot catch its own errors; the next boundary up handles them.

options.text: An error thrown while a child component renders
options.why: This is exactly what error boundaries are for.

options.text: An error thrown inside a child's `useEffect`
options.why: Errors in effects of descendants are caught by the nearest boundary too.

explanation: Error boundaries cover rendering, lifecycle methods and effects of the tree below them. They do not cover event handlers, asynchronous code such as timers, errors in the boundary itself, or server-side rendering errors.
reference: react.dev: Catching rendering errors with an error boundary

stem: A `<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>` boundary is showing loaded content. A normal (urgent) `setState` makes a child read a new, still-pending promise with `use()`. What happens to the old content?

options.text: React keeps showing the old content until the new data is ready
options.why: That happens for transitions. An urgent update that suspends shows the fallback instead.

options.text: The spinner appears; the old DOM stays mounted but hidden, so its state survives
options.why: React hides the existing children with display: none and shows the fallback beside them.

options.text: The spinner appears and the old children are unmounted, losing their state
options.why: Already-mounted children are hidden rather than unmounted, so their state is kept.

options.text: React throws an error, because suspending after content has appeared is not allowed
options.why: Re-suspending is allowed; it just shows the fallback again for an urgent update.

explanation: When an urgent update suspends inside an already-revealed boundary, React has no choice but to show the fallback. It keeps the old children mounted and hides them (style display: none), so local state and DOM are preserved for when the data arrives. Wrapping the update in startTransition avoids the fallback flash altogether.
reference: react.dev: <Suspense> (preventing already revealed content from hiding)

stem: Same boundary, but this time the update that makes the child suspend is wrapped: `startTransition(() => setUserId(next))`. What does the user see while the new user's data loads?

options.text: The previous user's content stays visible until the new content is ready
options.why: Transitions avoid hiding already-revealed content; React waits instead of falling back.

options.text: The `<Spinner />` fallback, exactly as with an urgent update
options.why: Transitions specifically prevent revealed content from being replaced by a fallback.

options.text: A blank region, because the old content is unmounted before the new render
options.why: Nothing is unmounted; the previous committed UI stays on screen.

options.text: Partially rendered new content with holes where the data is missing
options.why: React never commits a partially rendered tree for a suspended render.

explanation: Inside a transition, React prefers to keep the old UI rather than replace visible content with a fallback. It renders the new tree in the background and commits it once the suspended data resolves. Use isPending from useTransition to show that something is happening.

options.text: `lazy` only works with class components; convert `Chart` to a class
options.why: lazy works with function components; the problem is which export it reads.

options.text: The import path needs a file extension; write `import('./Chart.js')`
options.why: The module loads fine. React then looks for a default export and finds none.

options.text: `lazy` reads `.default`; use `import('./Chart').then(m => ({ default: m.Chart }))`
options.why: The module has only a named export, so the resolved default is undefined.

options.text: Lazy components must be wrapped in `memo` before React can render them, or the element type is rejected
options.why: memo is unrelated; lazy needs a module object with a default export.

explanation: lazy expects its loader to return a promise for a module object whose default export is a component. With only a named export, React receives undefined and throws "Element type is invalid... Lazy element type must resolve to a class or function." Re-export it as default, or map the named export to default in the loader.

stem: If a component fetches data in `useEffect` and stores it in state, wrapping that component in `<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>` makes the spinner appear until the data arrives.

options.text: True
options.why: Suspense cannot see work started in effects; the component has already rendered.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the component renders normally (usually with its own loading state), and the fallback never shows.

explanation: Suspense works when rendering itself suspends, for example through use() on a cached promise, lazy(), or a Suspense-enabled framework. An effect runs after the component has committed, so nothing ever suspends.

stem: A search box filters a very slow list. A developer writes `onChange={e => startTransition(() => setQuery(e.target.value))}` for the controlled `<input value={query}>`. What goes wrong, and what is the usual fix?

options.text: Nothing: transitions make the input itself render faster
options.why: Transitions change priority, not speed, and a controlled input needs its update applied immediately.

options.text: React throws because transitions cannot contain `setState` calls for controlled inputs like this one
options.why: setState calls are exactly what transitions are meant to wrap.

options.text: The input lags; keep `query` urgent and defer the list with `useDeferredValue`
options.why: Text input updates must be synchronous; only the slow derived UI should be deferred.

options.text: Typing triggers a Suspense fallback; add a boundary around the input
options.why: Nothing here suspends. The problem is that the input value itself is deferred.

explanation: Controlled text inputs must be updated synchronously, or the cursor and typed characters can fall out of sync. Keep the input state urgent and either derive a deferred value for the slow list (useDeferredValue) or use a second state variable updated inside a transition.

stem: An error boundary around a user profile shows "Something went wrong". When the user navigates to a different profile, the error message stays even though the new profile would render fine. What is the simplest fix?

options.text: Call `this.forceUpdate()` from the boundary when the URL changes
options.why: forceUpdate re-renders, but the boundary's error state is still set, so it shows the fallback again.

options.text: Render the boundary with `key={profileId}` so React remounts it for each profile
options.why: A new key creates a fresh boundary instance with no error state.

options.text: Wrap the boundary in `<Suspense>` so it retries automatically
options.why: Suspense handles waiting, not resetting errors.

options.text: Move the boundary inside the profile component, so the boundary re-runs and clears on every render
options.why: A boundary cannot catch errors from the component that renders it, only from its children.

explanation: An error boundary keeps its error state until it is reset. Changing its key remounts it with fresh state. Libraries like react-error-boundary also offer resetKeys and a resetErrorBoundary callback for the same purpose.

options.text: The spinner, because `Results` suspends on the new query
options.why: The new query only reaches Results in the background render, which keeps the old UI if it suspends.

options.text: The new text in the input, with the previous results still shown
options.why: The urgent render uses the old deferred value; the background render waits for data.

options.text: Nothing changes until the new results are ready, including the text in the input box itself
options.why: The input is updated urgently, so it changes immediately.

options.text: Both old and new results side by side while loading
options.why: React commits one version of Results, not both.

explanation: useDeferredValue first re-renders with the old value, so the input updates instantly and Results renders the old (already loaded) query. React then tries the new value in the background. If that render suspends, React keeps the stale results instead of showing the fallback, and swaps them in when ready.
reference: react.dev: useDeferredValue (showing stale content while fresh content is loading)

stem: React 19.2 added a built-in component that can hide part of the UI while keeping its state, and render it at low priority: `<______ mode={isVisible ? 'visible' : 'hidden'}>`. Type its name.
explanation: Activity with mode="hidden" hides its children (React applies display: none), unmounts their effects and keeps their state, so switching back is instant. It replaces patterns such as conditionally unmounting tabs and losing their state.

options.text: The spinner at full opacity
options.why: The boundary already shows user 1, and the update is a transition, so no fallback appears.

options.text: User 1's data, dimmed to 60% opacity
options.why: React commits an urgent render with isPending true while the transition renders in the background.

options.text: User 2's data dimmed, with placeholders for missing fields
options.why: React never commits a partially loaded render.

options.text: User 1's data at full opacity until user 2 is ready
options.why: isPending becomes true straight away, so the dimming does show.

explanation: startTransition schedules two things: an urgent render that flips isPending to true, and a background render with the new state. The background render suspends on user 2, so React keeps user 1 on screen, now dimmed, and commits the new UI when the data resolves.

options.text: Both keep showing Tab A on screen until all of Tab B's data has finished loading
options.why: App 2 reveals a brand-new inner boundary, and React is allowed to show new boundaries' fallbacks.

options.text: Both show "Loading page", because the outer boundary is the closest one
options.why: In a transition React does not hide already-revealed content behind the outer fallback.

options.text: App 1 keeps Tab A; App 2 shows "Tab B" with "Loading B" below it
options.why: Only already-visible content is protected; new boundaries may show their fallback immediately.

options.text: App 1 shows "Loading page"; App 2 keeps Tab A on screen
options.why: It is the other way round: App 1 has no new boundary to reveal.

explanation: During a transition React avoids hiding content that is already visible, but it happily shows fallbacks for boundaries that appear for the first time. In App 1 the only boundary is already showing Tab A, so React waits. In App 2 the new tab contains a new boundary, so React can commit the heading and "Loading B" right away. This is how you design navigations that reveal a layout immediately.
reference: react.dev: <Suspense> (preventing already revealed content from hiding)

stem: A team uses the standalone `import { startTransition } from 'react'` inside a data library (outside any component). What do they give up compared with `useTransition`?

options.text: The update is no longer interruptible, because only the hook marks transitions
options.why: The standalone function marks updates as transitions just like the hook does.

options.text: There is no `isPending` flag, so components cannot show that the transition is in progress
options.why: Standalone startTransition marks updates but reports no pending state.

options.text: Suspense boundaries will show their fallback instead of keeping old content
options.why: Already-revealed content is protected for both forms.

options.text: It runs the callback asynchronously, so state updates inside it are lost
options.why: The callback runs synchronously; updates inside it are marked as transitions.

explanation: React.startTransition behaves like the function returned by useTransition but cannot provide isPending, because there is no component to re-render with that flag. Use it where hooks are unavailable (routers, data libraries) and expose pending state some other way, or use the hook in components.

options.text: It becomes an unhandled promise rejection, because errors after an await escape React
options.why: React 19 tracks the action's promise and rethrows its rejection into the tree.

options.text: It is swallowed, and `isPending` just goes back to false
options.why: React does not hide action errors; it reports them to the nearest boundary.

options.text: The nearest error boundary catches it and shows "Failed"
options.why: Errors thrown by a transition's action are rethrown so the closest error boundary handles them.

options.text: It is caught only if `save` is also wrapped in try/catch inside `onClick`
options.why: onClick only starts the transition; the rejection surfaces later through React.

explanation: React 19 supports async functions in startTransition (actions). If the action throws or rejects, React treats it like a rendering error and shows the nearest error boundary. To show inline error messages instead, catch the error inside the action and store it in state (or use useActionState).
reference: react.dev: useTransition (displaying an error to users with an error boundary)

options.text: `use` only accepts promises returned by `async` functions, so rewrite the fetch call with `async/await`
options.why: Any promise works; the problem is that a new promise is created on every render.

options.text: The promise must be awaited before it is passed to `use`
options.why: Awaiting in a client component is not possible during render; use() exists to read pending promises.

options.text: Each render creates a new promise; create and cache it outside render instead
options.why: Pass a stable promise from a server component, a loader, or a cache keyed by postId.

options.text: `use` cannot be called with props; move `postId` into state first
options.why: Props are fine. Promise identity is what matters.

explanation: When a component suspends, React retries the render later. If render creates the promise, each retry gets a fresh pending promise and can keep suspending (and refetching). Promises passed to use() in client components should come from somewhere stable: a server component, a framework loader, or a cache that returns the same promise for the same key.

stem: A component assigns IDs with a module-level counter during render: `let next = 0; function Row() { const id = next++; ... }`. In production the IDs sometimes skip numbers, and in development every ID is off by one. Why?

options.text: The counter is shared between browser tabs through module caching, so other tabs consume IDs too
options.why: Each tab has its own JavaScript heap and module instances.

options.text: React may render more than once per commit: Strict Mode double-renders, and interrupted renders are discarded
options.why: Side effects in render run once per render attempt, not once per commit.

options.text: JavaScript integers overflow after a few thousand increments
options.why: Numbers stay exact up to 2^53; overflow is not the issue.

options.text: Hooks reset module variables between renders
options.why: Hooks do not touch module scope.

explanation: Render must be pure because React may render a component several times and commit only once: Strict Mode renders twice in development, and concurrent rendering can abandon renders that were interrupted or suspended. Mutating outside variables during render therefore leaks the extra attempts. Use useId for IDs, or move side effects into event handlers or effects.

stem: In React 19, `<Suspense fallback="Loading"><A /><B /></Suspense>` renders, and `A` suspends on its data. `B` would also suspend on separate data. What does React 19 do differently from React 18 here?

options.text: React 19 renders `B` fully before showing the fallback, so both requests start before anything is committed
options.why: That was closer to React 18. React 19 commits the fallback as soon as A suspends.

options.text: It commits the fallback once `A` suspends, then pre-renders the siblings to start `B`'s request
options.why: Fallbacks show sooner, and pre-warming still starts the sibling fetches.

options.text: It never renders `B` until `A`'s data has arrived, which creates a request waterfall between the two
options.why: React 19 pre-warms suspended siblings, so B's data starts loading before A resolves.

options.text: It shows `B` immediately, and the fallback only covers `A`'s slot
options.why: One boundary reveals its children together; it cannot show B while A is pending.

explanation: React 19 changed Suspense so the fallback commits immediately when a component suspends, without first rendering the rest of the siblings. After committing the fallback, React schedules a pre-warm render of the suspended siblings so their lazy code and data requests start in parallel. The boundary still reveals all its children together.
reference: React 19 release notes: improvements to Suspense

stem: During hydration, a component inside a `<Suspense>` boundary renders `new Date().toLocaleTimeString()`, so its text differs from the server HTML. A static `<header>` outside the boundary matches. What does React 19 do?

options.text: It patches only the mismatched text node and logs a warning
options.why: React no longer patches text mismatches; it regenerates the affected tree on the client.

options.text: It discards all of the server HTML and client-renders the whole page again, including the header
options.why: That happens when the mismatch is outside any Suspense boundary.

options.text: It client-renders only that Suspense boundary and keeps the hydrated header
options.why: Suspense boundaries limit how much server HTML a mismatch throws away.

options.text: It keeps the server text forever, because hydration never changes existing DOM
options.why: React makes the DOM match the client render, so the server text is replaced.

explanation: When hydration fails, React falls back to client rendering up to the nearest Suspense boundary and reports it through onRecoverableError (React 19 logs one error with a diff of the mismatch). Without a boundary, the whole root is client-rendered. Fix the cause (for example, render time-dependent text in an effect) rather than relying on the recovery.
reference: react.dev: hydrateRoot (handling different client and server content)

stem: A streamed SSR page has several Suspense boundaries that are hydrating. Which two statements about selective hydration in React 18+ are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Each boundary can hydrate as soon as its HTML and code arrive, without waiting for the rest of the page
options.why: Hydration is split into independent units per Suspense boundary.

options.text: If the user clicks inside a boundary that has not hydrated yet, React hydrates that boundary first
options.why: React prioritises boundaries the user is interacting with.

options.text: All JavaScript for the page must load before any boundary can hydrate
options.why: That was the pre-18 model that selective hydration replaced.

options.text: Clicks on not-yet-hydrated content are lost and must be repeated
options.why: React records discrete events like clicks and replays them after hydrating that boundary.

options.text: Selective hydration only works when every boundary has finished streaming
options.why: It specifically works while other boundaries are still streaming.

explanation: With streaming SSR and hydrateRoot, Suspense boundaries hydrate independently. React prioritises a boundary the user interacts with and replays discrete events once it has hydrated, so slow parts of the page do not block interactivity elsewhere.
reference: React 18 working group: New Suspense SSR architecture

stem: A server streams a page with `renderToPipeableStream`, and a `<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}><Comments /></Suspense>` section waits for slow data. Put the steps in order.

options.text: The server sends the shell HTML with the spinner in the comments slot
The comments data resolves on the server and React renders that boundary
The server streams the comments HTML plus a small inline script into the same response
The inline script swaps the spinner for the comments HTML in the DOM
The boundary hydrates once its client code has loaded

explanation: Streaming lets the browser display the shell immediately. Late boundaries arrive as extra HTML in the same response, together with a tiny script that inserts them where their fallback was, even before React hydrates. Hydration of that boundary then happens independently once its JavaScript is available.

stem:
Both components suspend on separate requests. The posts data arrives first, then the header data. What is on screen after the posts arrive, and after the header arrives?

```jsx
<Suspense fallback="Loading page">
  <Header />                                {/* suspends on A */}
  <Suspense fallback="Loading posts">
    <Posts />                                {/* suspends on B */}
  </Suspense>
</Suspense>
```

options.text: Posts appear with "Loading page" above them, then the header fills in
options.why: The outer boundary is still suspended, so nothing inside it, including the inner boundary, is shown.

options.text: "Loading page" stays until the header loads; then header and posts appear together
options.why: The inner boundary only becomes visible when its parent boundary reveals.

options.text: "Loading posts" replaces the page fallback first, then the header appears
options.why: The inner fallback is part of the outer boundary's content, which is not shown yet.

options.text: The header area stays empty while posts show, because boundaries are independent
options.why: Nested boundaries reveal from the outside in; the inner one cannot show before its parent.

explanation: Nested Suspense boundaries reveal from the outside in. While Header suspends, the whole outer boundary shows "Loading page". Posts may finish early, but they are inside the outer boundary, so they appear only when the outer content (including Header) is ready. If Posts were still pending at that point, "Loading posts" would show in their place.
reference: react.dev: <Suspense> (revealing nested content as it loads)

options.text: Only one render with `'react'`, because `initialValue` is ignored on mount
options.why: In React 19 initialValue is used for exactly this initial render.

options.text: A first render with `''`, then a background re-render with `'react'`
options.why: With an initialValue, the deferred value starts there and catches up in the background.

options.text: A first render with `'react'`, then a second render with `''`
options.why: The value moves from the initial value towards the latest one, never the reverse.

options.text: Only one render with `''` until `query` changes for the first time
options.why: React schedules a background render with the latest value straight after mount.

explanation: React 19 added an optional initialValue to useDeferredValue. On mount the component renders with that value (cheap, for example an empty list) and React immediately schedules a background render with the real value. Without initialValue there is nothing to defer on mount, so it renders the real value directly.

stem: A tab panel is wrapped in `<Activity mode={active ? 'visible' : 'hidden'}>`. The panel has a counter in `useState` and a `useEffect` that subscribes to a socket. The user increments the counter to 5, switches tabs, then switches back. What happened in between?

options.text: The panel unmounted; the counter is back to 0 and the effect re-subscribes
options.why: Activity preserves state, which is the point of using it instead of conditional rendering.

options.text: Its DOM was hidden and its effects cleaned up; the counter is still 5
options.why: Hidden Activity keeps state but tears down effects until it becomes visible again.

options.text: Nothing changed: hidden panels keep their effects and socket subscriptions running in the background
options.why: Effects are unmounted while hidden, so subscriptions stop.

options.text: The panel was moved to a detached DOM tree and re-attached on return
options.why: React keeps the DOM in place and hides it with display: none.

explanation: In hidden mode, Activity hides its children with display: none, runs effect cleanups (so subscriptions and timers stop) and keeps component state. Updates to hidden content render at a lower priority. When it becomes visible again, the DOM is shown and effects are set up again.

stem: Which two statements about transitions are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: An urgent update (such as typing) can interrupt a transition render that is in progress
options.why: React abandons the in-progress transition render, handles the urgent update, then restarts the transition.

options.text: `setState` calls inside a `setTimeout` callback started from within `startTransition` are not marked as transitions
options.why: Only updates made while the startTransition callback is running are marked; the timer fires later.

options.text: Transitions run the render on a background thread so the main thread stays free
options.why: React renders on the main thread; it yields between units of work instead.

options.text: Transitions delay network requests until the browser is idle
options.why: Transitions affect rendering priority, not when fetches start.

options.text: A transition that suspends always shows the nearest Suspense fallback
options.why: Already-revealed content stays visible during a transition.

explanation: Transitions mark updates as non-urgent. React renders them in small chunks on the main thread and gives way to urgent updates. Only updates scheduled while the callback is running are marked, so a setTimeout inside startTransition loses the mark unless you call startTransition inside the timer as well.

stem: Several components read a global store with `store.getState()` during render and subscribe in `useEffect`. With concurrent rendering, users sometimes see two components showing different values for the same store at once. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: This is tearing: the store changed in the middle of an interruptible render
options.why: Different components read the store at different moments of one render.

options.text: Reading the store with `useSyncExternalStore` fixes it
options.why: It makes React detect changes during render and re-render synchronously for a consistent snapshot.

options.text: It is caused by React batching state updates, so `flushSync` on every change fixes it
options.why: Batching applies to React state, and flushSync everywhere would hurt performance without fixing reads in render.

options.text: Wrapping each reader in `memo` prevents it
options.why: memo skips re-renders, which can make stale reads worse.

options.text: It cannot happen in React 18 or later, because rendering is synchronous
options.why: Concurrent rendering is interruptible, which is exactly why tearing became possible.

explanation: Concurrent rendering can pause between components. If a mutable external store changes during that gap, components read different values in the same render: a "tear". useSyncExternalStore gives React a subscribe function and a snapshot getter, so it can detect a change during render and fall back to a synchronous, consistent render.

stem: A boundary `<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>` is already showing content. Match each way a child suspends on new data with what the user sees.

options.text: Spinner replaces the content, which stays mounted but hidden
options.why: Urgent updates show the fallback.

options.text: Old content stays visible until the new content is ready
options.why: Transitions protect revealed content.

options.text: The new section appears with its own fallback right away
options.why: New boundaries may show their fallback.

options.text: Stale content stays visible while the fresh content renders in the background
options.why: Deferred values keep the previous render.

prompts.text: A plain `setState` from a click handler
A transition that reveals a newly mounted inner `<Suspense>`
The child receives a value from `useDeferredValue`

explanation: React chooses between showing a fallback and keeping old UI based on the kind of update. Urgent updates must show something, so they fall back. Transitions and deferred values prefer keeping what is already on screen. A boundary that has never been shown can display its fallback even during a transition.

stem: A user clicks a tab, which starts a slow transition render of a 5,000-row table. Halfway through that render, they type into a search box (an urgent update). What does React do?

options.text: Finishes the table render first, then handles the keystroke
options.why: That is the blocking behaviour transitions were designed to avoid.

options.text: Commits the half-rendered table, then applies the keystroke
options.why: React never commits a partially rendered tree.

options.text: Abandons the unfinished table render, commits the keystroke, then restarts the transition
options.why: Urgent updates interrupt transitions; the transition is retried from the start.

options.text: Renders the keystroke on a second thread while the table render continues in parallel on the first
options.why: React has one render thread; it yields rather than running in parallel.

explanation: Transition renders yield to the browser regularly. When an urgent update arrives, React throws away the unfinished transition render, renders and commits the urgent update, and then starts the transition render again using the newest state. This is why render must be pure: the abandoned work must leave no trace.
reference: react.dev: useTransition (marking a state update as a non-blocking transition)

options.text: Tab 2, briefly, before tab 3 replaces it when its data arrives
options.why: React does not commit the intermediate tab; the pending transitions resolve to the latest state.

options.text: Still tab 1 with `isPending` true, until tab 3's data arrives
options.why: React batches pending transitions and renders the latest state, which is still suspended.

options.text: The Suspense fallback, because two transitions conflict
options.why: Concurrent transitions do not cause fallbacks for revealed content.

options.text: Tab 3 with missing data, because the latest update always wins immediately
options.why: Suspended renders are never committed.

explanation: When several transitions are pending, React currently batches them and works toward the latest state. Tab 2 becoming ready does not matter, because the target is tab 3, which is still suspended. The old tab stays visible with isPending true until tab 3 can be committed.
reference: react.dev: useTransition (caveats on multiple ongoing transitions)

options.text: The Editor chunk is re-downloaded on every keystroke
options.why: The browser caches the module, so the network request is not repeated.

options.text: Each render creates a new lazy component type, so Editor remounts and re-suspends
options.why: A new type breaks identity: state is lost and the boundary falls back each time.

options.text: `setText` is an urgent update, so it always triggers the Suspense fallback for every child beneath it
options.why: Urgent updates only show a fallback if something suspends, and here the cause is the new type.

options.text: Suspense must be outside `Page` for lazy components to work
options.why: The placement is fine; the lazy() call is in the wrong scope.

explanation: Calling lazy() inside render returns a brand-new component type on every render. React sees a different type, unmounts the old Editor (losing its state), mounts the new one, and because the new lazy type has not resolved yet, the boundary briefly shows its fallback. Declare lazy components at module scope.

stem: Promises are cached in a module-level `Map` keyed by URL and read with `use()`. One request rejects, and the error boundary shows a "Try again" button that resets the boundary (via a new `key`). The retry fails instantly every time, even after the server recovers. Why?

options.text: Error boundaries cannot be reset while a promise is rejected
options.why: Resetting the boundary works; the remounted child just reads the same promise again.

options.text: `use()` caches rejections internally per component instance, so remounting the child cannot clear them
options.why: use() reads whatever promise you pass; the stale rejection comes from your own cache.

options.text: The cache still holds the rejected promise, so the retry rethrows it; evict it first
options.why: A rejected promise stays rejected, so the cache must drop it to allow a new request.

options.text: The boundary needs `getDerivedStateFromProps` to clear the error
options.why: The boundary resets fine; the data source is what still fails.

explanation: A settled promise never changes. If the cache returns the same rejected promise, every render after a reset reads that rejection and throws again. Retry logic must invalidate the cache entry (or store a fresh promise) as part of the reset, for example in react-error-boundary's onReset callback.

stem: A list renders 20 items, each in its own `<Suspense>` boundary. Their data resolves a few milliseconds apart, yet the items appear in a couple of batches rather than one by one, slightly after their data arrives. What explains this?

options.text: Each boundary waits for all sibling boundaries to resolve first
options.why: Sibling boundaries are independent; nothing forces them to wait for each other.

options.text: React throttles Suspense reveals (about 300 ms) so close boundaries appear together
options.why: Throttling reduces layout jumps by batching reveals that land close together.

options.text: The browser coalesces DOM writes until the next garbage collection
options.why: Garbage collection does not control when DOM updates are made.

options.text: React shows suspended content only after every lazy chunk in the whole app has finished loading
options.why: Boundaries reveal independently; there is no global wait.

explanation: To avoid a jittery cascade of tiny layout changes, React throttles how often it reveals suspended content (currently around 300 ms in React's implementation). Boundaries that resolve close together are revealed in the same commit. If you need items to appear in a strict order, nest boundaries or use a single boundary instead.

stem: React 19 added options to `createRoot` and `hydrateRoot` for reporting errors. Which three statements are correct? (Choose three.)

options.text: `onCaughtError` runs when an error boundary catches an error
options.why: Use it to log errors that a boundary has already handled.

options.text: `onUncaughtError` runs when an error is not caught by any boundary
options.why: React then unmounts the root, and this is your last chance to report it.

options.text: `onRecoverableError` runs when React recovers on its own, such as a hydration mismatch it fixes by client rendering
options.why: These errors don't break the UI but usually point to a bug.

options.text: `onCaughtError` also fires for errors thrown in event handlers
options.why: Event handler errors never reach error boundaries, so they are not "caught" errors.

options.text: Setting these options replaces the need for error boundaries
options.why: They report errors; only boundaries render fallback UI.

explanation: React 19 reports errors once instead of logging them twice, and lets you route them to monitoring: onCaughtError for errors handled by a boundary, onUncaughtError for errors that reach the root, and onRecoverableError for errors React recovered from automatically. None of them render UI; boundaries still do that.

stem: A route renders `<Suspense key={userId} fallback={<Spinner />}><Profile userId={userId} /></Suspense>`. Navigation to a new user is wrapped in `startTransition`, and the profile data is not loaded yet. What does the user see?

options.text: The previous user's profile, because transitions keep revealed content
options.why: The key makes it a different boundary, so the old one is not "already revealed" content any more.

options.text: The spinner, because the new key creates a brand-new boundary that may show its fallback
options.why: A changed key resets the boundary, and new boundaries can show fallbacks during transitions.

options.text: A blank area where the profile was, until the new user's data arrives and React can commit it
options.why: React shows the new boundary's fallback rather than nothing.

options.text: An error, because `key` is not a valid prop on `Suspense`
options.why: key works on any element, including Suspense.

explanation: Transitions only avoid hiding content that is already revealed. Giving the boundary a new key unmounts the old boundary and mounts a fresh one, and a newly mounted boundary is allowed to show its fallback. The docs use exactly this pattern on purpose, to reset a profile page's loading state when the user changes.

options.text: Also wrap `setText` in `startTransition`, so that both the input and the list become non-urgent
options.why: That defers the input itself, which makes typing worse.

options.text: Wrap `SlowList` in `memo` so the urgent render can skip it
options.why: Without memo, the urgent render still re-renders SlowList, which defeats the deferral.

options.text: Pass `text` instead of `deferredText` to `SlowList`
options.why: That removes the deferral entirely.

options.text: Put `SlowList` inside `<Suspense>`
options.why: Nothing suspends; Suspense would not change render cost.

explanation: useDeferredValue gives you an urgent render where the deferred value is still the old one, followed by a background render with the new value. That only helps if the urgent render can skip the slow component. Since App re-renders, SlowList re-renders too unless it is wrapped in memo, which bails out because its prop has not changed.
reference: react.dev: useDeferredValue (deferring re-rendering for a part of the UI)

stem: With streaming SSR, if a component inside a `<Suspense>` boundary throws on the server, React sends that boundary's fallback HTML and retries rendering the component on the client.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: the server error is reported (onError), and the client tries again; only a client-side failure reaches an error boundary.

options.text: False
options.why: React does not fail the whole response for an error inside a boundary; it falls back and retries on the client.

explanation: When a component inside a Suspense boundary throws during server rendering, React does not abort the page. It streams the fallback for that boundary, calls the server onError callback, and tries to render the component again on the client. If it fails on the client too, the nearest error boundary handles it. Errors in the shell (outside any boundary) call onShellError instead.
reference: react.dev: renderToPipeableStream (recovering from errors outside the shell)

stem: Which two pieces of render-time code are unsafe under concurrent rendering, even though they seem to work in simple tests? (Choose two.)

options.text: `analytics.track('viewed', id)` called directly in the component body
options.why: A render may be thrown away (interrupted or suspended), so the view is logged for UI that never appeared.

options.text: `cache[id] = expensive(id)` writing into a shared module-level object during render
options.why: Abandoned or duplicated renders mutate shared state that other renders then see.

options.text: `const total = items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0)`
options.why: A pure calculation from props is exactly what render is for.

options.text: `const [open, setOpen] = useState(false)`
options.why: Declaring state is pure; React manages it.

options.text: `const id = useId()`
options.why: useId is designed to be stable and safe across renders and hydration.

explanation: React may start, pause, abandon and repeat renders. Anything with an observable side effect (logging, mutating shared objects, subscriptions) must move into effects or event handlers, where it runs once per commit. Pure calculations and hook declarations are safe.

stem: In React 19.2+ (no Strict Mode), `<Suspense fallback="Loading"><A /><B /></Suspense>` is rendered. `A` and `B` each suspend on their own pending promise, and both promises stay pending. How many times has `A`'s function body run when the fallback is on screen and pre-warming has finished? Type a number.
explanation: First render: A runs and suspends, and React 19 commits the fallback straight away without rendering B. Pre-warm render: React renders the suspended siblings again in the background (A, then B) so all their data requests start. That is 2 runs of A and 1 of B, which is why components must not count on rendering exactly once.
reference: React 19 release notes: improvements to Suspense

stem: In React 19, a component runs `startTransition(async () => { await save(); setCount(1); })` from a button, and `count` is 0. Put the committed renders in order (`isPending` shown as P).

options.text: `count 0`, not pending (before the click)
`count 0`, P: the urgent render that sets `isPending`
`count 1`, P: the update after `await` commits while the action is still pending
`count 1`, not pending: the action's promise has settled

explanation: isPending turns true immediately and stays true for the whole async action. React 19 cannot yet carry the transition context across an await, so setCount(1) after the await is not marked as a transition: it renders on its own while the action is still pending. Then the action resolves and isPending becomes false. Wrap updates after an await in another startTransition if they should be part of the transition.
reference: react.dev: useTransition (react doesn't treat my state update after await as a transition)
